report.summary: Cross-language code indexing in 2025-2026 is dominated by SCIP (Source Code Index Protocol) as the successor to LSIF, with tree-sitter and stack-graphs serving complementary roles. SCIP is the preferred format for precise, language-agnostic indexing, supported by Sourcegraph and GitHub. LSIF is legacy but still used. Tree-sitter provides fast, incremental parsing for many languages but lacks full semantic resolution. Stack-graphs (from GitHub) enable cross-file navigation without a build system. Production-grade indexers exist for Go, TypeScript, Java, Python, Rust, C/C++, Ruby, and JavaScript
risks: Tree-sitter grammars for Fortran and Verilog may be incomplete or unmaintained.
SCIP indexers require language-specific semantic analysis; heuristics may miss complex references.
No existing SCIP indexer for LaTeX; custom development needed.
todos: Evaluate tree-sitter grammars for Fortran (tree-sitter-fortran) and Verilog (tree-sitter-verilog).
Check fortls for LSIF output capability; if yes, convert LSIF to SCIP.
For LaTeX, prototype a SCIP indexer using texlab's parser or a simple TeX tokenizer.
Consider stack-graphs for cross-file references in Verilog (module instantiation).

handoff.suggestion: Start by running tree-sitter queries on a sample Fortran codebase to extract function/subroutine definitions and calls. If coverage is acceptable, emit SCIP documents. For Verilog, use tree-sitter-verilog to extract module ports and instantiations. For LaTeX, use a regex-based approach to find \label and \ref, then emit SCIP. This gives a minimal viable indexer in days, not months.
